purpose: Extend blueprints/gap-resolution-20260922/restic-filesystem-semantics/fixture.py (reused unmodified via blueprints/gap-wave2-20260923/restic-mtime-sparse-uid/extend_fixture.py) with the three items open_gaps[recovery-portability][6] still lists as unmeasured: timestamps (mtime/atime), UID/GID ownership variation via a real chown, and sparse-block preservation on restore (`restic restore --sparse` vs plain restore, measured with `du`).
preregistered: If a deterministic-timestamp, chowned-file fixture backed up and restored twice (once plain, once with --sparse) shows: (a) mtime preserved exactly on both restores, (b) atime NOT preserved (restore sets atime to restore time, not the original), (c) UID/GID NOT restored to the chowned owner when running as a non-root user (a known restic/POSIX limitation requiring root), and (d) `--sparse` measurably reduces allocated disk blocks for the 10MiB sparse file relative to a plain restore (which fully materializes it), while both restores remain content-identical (same sha256) to the source, this settles the sparse/UID-varied/timestamp portion of open_gaps[6] as measured (all four outcomes confirmed rather than assumed). If instead mtime is NOT preserved, or `--sparse` shows no measurable block reduction versus plain restore, that would refute part of this fixture-extension's working assumptions and must be recorded as a failure. `sudo -n true` gates the chown step; if it fails, chown is recorded as not runnable rather than skipped silently.

correction_2026-09-23.finding: A fix-round review found that the original atime measurement below (commands at indices 3, 8, 9, and their reflection in `result`) was invalid: manifest_with_timestamps() in extend_fixture.py called fixture.manifest() (which reads every file's bytes via p.read_bytes() to compute sha256) BEFORE its own lstat() pass. On this scratch filesystem (ext4, relatime), reading a file whose current atime predates its ctime -- true immediately after os.utime() stamps a fixed reference atime, and true immediately after a restic restore -- moves atime to the time of that read. So both the recorded 'before' atime (1790126920) and 'after' atime (1790126937) were the manifest tool's own read times, not the fixture's stamped value (1700000500) or a genuine post-restore value. The word 'documented behaviour' in the original preregistration/result was also an unverified assumption, not something this receipt had checked against restic's actual documentation, and has been removed.
correction_2026-09-23.fix_applied: blueprints/gap-wave2-20260923/restic-mtime-sparse-uid/extend_fixture.py was changed so manifest_with_timestamps() does its own lstat() pass FIRST (lstat never touches atime, only open/read does) and calls fixture.manifest() afterward, once the genuine timestamps are already captured.
correction_2026-09-23.rerun_preregistration: With the corrected lstat-before-read ordering, the corrected before-manifest should show atime=1700000500 (the stamped reference value) on every file entry, not a self-inflicted bumped value; the prior run's before-manifest showed a uniform ~1790126920 value on every entry instead, which is itself evidence of the bug (a real stamped-then-untouched atime would not equalize across ten independently-stamped files to within the same few seconds as 'now'). If the corrected before-manifest instead still shows a uniform current-time value, the bug would not be confirmed and the original finding would need separate investigation. Given the corrected before-manifest, if the after-restore manifest's atime differs from 1700000500 and instead reflects restore time, that is now a validly measured (not self-inflicted) confirmation that restic does not preserve atime on restore; if it matches 1700000500, that would refute the original conclusion entirely.
correction_2026-09-23.rerun_result: The corrected before-manifest showed atime=1700000500 on 11 of 12 entries (all 10 files plus the symlink), confirming the bug: the original run's uniform ~1790126920 'before' value was indeed a self-inflicted post-read artifact, not the stamped value. One entry, the empty directory, still showed a current-time atime (1790127736) even in the corrected run -- rglob() must open/read a directory's contents to recurse into it, and that opendir/readdir itself counts as an access of the directory, so a directory's atime cannot be captured by this traversal-based approach without also being touched by the same traversal; this is a structural limitation of the fixture, not a code-ordering bug, and is now recorded as a limitation rather than folded into the file-level atime claim. For the 11 correctly-captured entries, the after-restore atime was 1790127758 (restore time) for all of them, differing from the stamped 1700000500 -- a validly measured confirmation, this time not an artifact of the check's own methodology, that restic 0.19.1 restore sets atime to restore time rather than preserving the original. mtime remained exactly preserved (1700000000, unchanged) in both the buggy and corrected runs, so the mtime conclusion was never affected by this bug. The UID/GID and sparse-block-reduction findings are also unaffected: neither depends on the atime-capture ordering.

correction_2026-09-23.corrected_conclusion: The original receipt's substantive atime-not-preserved conclusion happened to be directionally correct, but was reached through an invalid measurement (a self-inflicted read-before-lstat bug that made both 'before' and 'after' show near-identical current-time values, which coincidentally still diffed by a few seconds and so still showed as 'changed'). tool_versions.restic: 0.19.1 (pre-existing pinned install, not installed by this check)

result: CORRECTED 2026-09-23 (see correction_2026-09-23 above; original wording below is retained for the record but its atime portion was invalid as originally measured). restic 0.19.1 preserves mtime exactly across both plain and --sparse restores (a fixed 1700000000 reference timestamp round-tripped with zero diff). It does NOT preserve atime for plain files: the original measurement of this claim was invalid (a self-inflicted read-before-lstat ordering bug in the check's own helper made both the 'before' and 'after' readings reflect the helper's own read times rather than genuine values), but a corrected rerun with fixed lstat-before-read ordering independently confirms the same directional conclusion -- 11 of 12 fixture entries (all files and the symlink) showed a correctly-captured stamped atime of 1700000500 before restore and 1790127758 (restore time) after, on both restore modes. The 12th entry (an empty directory) has a separate, structural limitation: recursively traversing a directory to build the manifest requires opening/reading it, which itself updates the directory's atime regardless of lstat ordering, so this check cannot validly measure directory atime preservation at all. restic does NOT restore UID/GID ownership when running as a non-root user (the chowned plain.txt, owner nobody:nobody (65534:65534) at backup time, comes back owned by the invoking user seath (1000:1000) on both restore modes) -- unaffected by the atime bug, and matches known restic/POSIX behaviour for a non-root restore, though this receipt did not independently verify restic's own documentation states this. Content integrity (sha256), symlink targets, ACL text, xattrs and hardlink grouping were unaffected by either finding, matching the original gap-resolution-20260922 receipt's local round-trip result. For sparse-block preservation: the source sparse.bin used 8 of 20480 apparent 512-byte blocks; a plain `restic restore` fully materializes it to 20480/20480 (no sparseness preserved), while `restic restore --sparse` produces 1024/20480 -- a real, substantial (20x) reduction in allocated blocks versus the plain restore, though not as sparse as the original source file. (Neither the UID/GID nor sparse-block findings depend on the atime-capture ordering and were not rerun.)

verdict_impact.explanation: Measures three of open_gaps[6]'s previously-unmeasured items (timestamps, UID/GID, sparse-block preservation) with concrete, reproducible results instead of leaving them as assumptions. The atime portion required a fix-round correction (see correction_2026-09-23): the original measurement was invalid due to a read-before-lstat ordering bug in the check's own helper, but a corrected rerun independently reaches the same directional conclusion (atime not preserved for files) through a valid measurement, while also surfacing a separate structural limitation (directory atime cannot be measured by a recursive-traversal manifest at all, since the traversal itself reads the directory). UID/GID and sparse-block findings are unaffected by the bug and stand as originally measured. This narrows open_gaps[6] further (from 'advanced_by_receipt' toward closer to fully measured for the local-filesystem subset) without closing the remaining Windows-native-NTFS and long-term-retention items, which stay out of scope for this same-day check.

limitations: Single run per restore mode, no retry-to-fish per the preregistration rule (the atime portion required one corrected rerun after a fix-round review found the original measurement invalid; see correction_2026-09-23 -- this is a methodology correction, not a retry-to-fish for a different outcome, since the corrected rerun reached the same directional conclusion).
Native NTFS-on-Windows and long-term retention remain untested, matching the original restic-filesystem-semantics receipt's own stated scope.
The chown target was a single file (plain.txt) to uid/gid 65534 (nobody); other entries' ownership was not varied.
atime comparisons use whole-second granularity (int(st_atime)); this does not test sub-second timestamp fidelity.

Passwordless sudo was available on this host (`sudo -n true` exit 0); a host without it would have made the chown step 'not runnable' per this check's own preregistered gating, and that branch was not exercised here since it succeeded.

The --sparse restore's 1024-vs-source's-8 block gap suggests restic's sparse-restore heuristic does not reproduce the exact original hole pattern; this receipt measures the block-count difference but does not fully characterize restic's sparse-detection algorithm.

Directory atime cannot be validly measured by this fixture's recursive-traversal manifest approach: building the manifest requires opening/reading each directory's contents to recurse into it, and that access itself updates the directory's atime regardless of lstat-vs-read ordering. The one directory entry (empty-dir) in both the original and corrected runs shows a current-time 'before' atime for this structural reason, not a code bug; only the 11 file/symlink entries' atime measurements are valid.

The corrected rerun used a fresh scratch fixture tree and repository (restic-fs-ext-atime-fix/), not the original run's artifacts, so the original raw_artifacts below remain as originally captured (including their invalid atime values) for the record; the corrected artifacts are listed separately.
